📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:.

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow, thank you for staying with us. Tschüss!

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.

Pistorius stated ‌criticism of ​Ukraine's deep strikes in ​Russia was ​misplaced.

In particular, Pistorius responded to US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby, who mentioned Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war.".

The German defense minister said "criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets" was "quite a ​stupid thing.".

Sources indicate that "Instead ‌of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on... energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius said.

He added that attacks inside ⁠Russia ​against ​non-civilian targets ​and sites used ‌by the military ​are ⁠legal and legitimate targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Former US President Joe Biden's latest autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.

Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts.".

"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel.".

Merkel and Trump were often at odds over issues tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.

Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she promptly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a initiative by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers ​to a deportation hub ​in ‌Rwanda.

Türk stated he had not yet ‌seen the draft proposal ‌but that ​his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by ​the proposed transfer of people from five ⁠European Union ​countries to ​Rwanda, where they have no ​genuine connection and ‌which has its own set ​of ⁠human rights challenges.".

Instead, he called ⁠for ​a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights.".

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl noted on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).

Upcoming figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.

Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.

According to recent reports, france was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.

According to recent reports, the Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.

Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%)  had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.

Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.

Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.

The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.

In a recent development, VC said that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.

"The ball is now in the employer's court," VC stated in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.

Lufthansa, meanwhile, noted it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 upcoming cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.

VC stated it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.

The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.

The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.

Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.

Sources indicate that the ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.

The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, said the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.

According to recent reports, the ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.

Spranger remarked the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, revealed prepares to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck.".

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp stated that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

Sources indicate that "Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support.".

In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it stated.

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's looks are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he stated.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals.".

The announcement of the looks comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

The strategy to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion,  German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on Tuesday.

He said that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.

Most of the new funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius stated in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.

He remarked Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously announced, as well as newly introduced radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.

He also mentioned that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.

Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.

He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has stated he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.

He mentioned Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it key for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.

Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and upcoming transport links.

Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.

He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.

In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.

Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.

The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.

The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.

Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that  sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the Upcoming York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents.".

It also stated that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank.".

The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.

The commission mentioned stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.

The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.

Some 286,000 new businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).

The BVR remarked the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.

However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.

In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.

The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.

The association also said that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.

DW's newsroom on the Rhine in Bonn wishes all readers a guten Tag!

Plans announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Leeds United and Tottenham Hotspur at Elland Road. The home side, lions at night and mice in the morning, have the unenviable record of 21 top-flight matches with a kick-off time before 3pm without a win. All that extra TV moolah comes in handy but their home ground, a bearpit under the floodlights, is neutered when its denizens are yawning instead of being fired up by social lubricant.

Daniel Farke’s team started the campaign well but are now without a win in five, drawing three matches with teams beneath them in the table – Crystal Palace, Manchester United and Sunderland – and  losing to two above them, Arsenal and Bournemouth. In fairness they played well against the champions for an hour and were deservedly in the lead until Mikel Arteta turnd to his billionaire’s bench and changed the game. At Bournemouth last week they also made a decent start, had a goal disallowed for striking Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s arm and then James Trafford chucked one in.

Industry observers note that they never recovered, found themselves increasingly bogged down when trying to unlock a low block and were mugged on the break in added time to lose 2-0. They are a robust side overly reliant on their wing-backs to create chances for their No 9 in the absence of the injured Noah Okafor who was unavailable to train with the team this week because of a groin injury but may be fit enough for the bench.

Spurs, by contrast, are buoyant following three wins on the bounce – over Coventry, Chelsea and Palace, two with clean sheets – that has taken them from 19th to ninth, three places above Leeds. They have won their last three visits to Elland Road, 0-4 under Antonio Conte, which proved to be the last match of Marcelo Bielsa’s glorious spell at the Peacocks, 1-4 under Ryan Mason, which sealed Leeds’ relegation, and 1-2 under Tomas Frank last year by virtue of goals from Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus as the home side struggled against their width back in the days before their switch to a back three.

It has been revealed that tel also scored in Spurs’ home game, a 1-1 draw in May, and then kicked Ethan Ampadu in the head to concede the penalty from which Leeds equalised. I wonder what kind of impact he will have today. Incidentally Roberto De Zerbi on his last visit to Leeds when manager of Brighton in 2022-23 had such a strop on the touchline when the home team equalised that he was within a gnat’s whisker of being sent off.

The Premier League is set to introduce a new LGBTQ+ inclusion campaign after ending its partnership with Stonewall, the charity behind the widely recognised Rainbow Laces initiative.

Recent findings suggest that stonewallâs Rainbow Laces campaign, rolled out in 2013, became a fixture across English football, with players from all Premier League clubs wearing rainbow-coloured laces and captains donning rainbow armbands to promote acceptance and equality. The campaign aimed to support LGBTQ+ rights and foster inclusivity among fans and young people.

After over a decade of collaboration, the league will now lead its own campaign, timed to coincide with LGBTQ+ History Month in February, The Telegraph report.

"Rainbow Laces has benefited from a wide range of partners with a natural ebb and flow reflecting cultural and sporting changes," a Stonewall spokesperson told BBC Sport.

"Alongside other sporting bodies the FA has been instrumental in advancing LGBTQ+ inclusion at the grassroots level and more recently the Women's Super League has taken up the mantle as the women's game has grown - enabling Rainbow Laces to reach more diverse audiences.".

Despite Stonewall's efforts, recent reports from Kick It Out reveal an alarming increase in discriminatory incidents in football, including rises in sexism, transphobia and faith-based abuse, with racism continuing to be the most prevalent glitch.

Controversies around playersâ attitudes to rainbow armbands have also made headlines. Last season, Ipswich captain Sam Morsy declined to wear one due to religious beliefs, while Crystal Palaceâs Marc GuÃ©hi faced criticism for personalising his armband with the phrase âI Love Jesus.â.

Additionally, Manchester United scrapped aims for LGBTQ+ support jackets after a player refused to participate.

With no openly gay or bisexual players presently in the Premier League, and the surge in discriminatory incidents, some question the timing of the split from Stonewall â an organisation highly respected for its work in LGBTQ+ advocacy.

Details of the Premier Leagueâs fresh campaign are still under wraps, but as the league presses âreset,â thereâs hope it will introduce a meaningful and effective initiative that advances equality rather than undermines it.

  • The revised planning framework, brought forward by Peel Waters, will guide the next phase of development across the 60-hectare site stretching from Everton's headquarters at The Royal Liver Building to the Club’s newly introduced waterfront home at Bramley-Moore Dock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that liverpool City Council has approved an updated Liverpool Waters masterplan, marking another significant milestone in the regeneration of the city’s northern waterfront and building on the transformation brought about by the development of Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium. The revised planning framework, brought forward by Peel Waters, will guide the next phase of development across the 60-hectare site stretching from Everton's headquarters at The Royal Liver Building to the Club’s new waterfront home at Bramley-Moore Dock. The development of Hill Dickinson Stadium has acted as a catalyst for the regeneration of North Liverpool, stimulating investment, creating employment opportunities, attracting visitors and unlocking the potential of a previously underutilised area of the city. The updated masterplan reflects the significant changes that have taken place along Liverpool’s waterfront since the original planning consent was granted in 2013, most notably the development of Everton’s new home and its emergence as a major sporting, entertainment and visitor destination. The refreshed intends will support the delivery of new homes, including affordable housing, alongside high-quality public spaces, healthcare provision, community facilities, employment opportunities and sustainable infrastructure across five distinctive waterfront neighbourhoods. Central to the plans is the creation of a new five-acre waterfront park at Central Docks. Already under construction as part of Liverpool Waters’ £81 million infrastructure investment programme, the park will feature more than 3,000 trees and is expected to open in spring 2028. The park and wider development will provide new and enhanced pedestrian routes through the northern docks, offering supporters and visitors an optional attractive walking route between Liverpool city centre and Hill Dickinson Stadium. Alongside new leisure and hospitality destinations, the creation of these public spaces will help transform the matchday and non-matchday journey for Evertonians, providing more opportunities for supporters to spend time along the waterfront before and after fixtures and major events at the stadium. The increased focus on pedestrian connectivity, active travel and sustainable transport also complements Everton’s ongoing work with key stakeholders to improve accessibility to Hill Dickinson Stadium and better connect the Club’s waterfront home with the city centre and surrounding communities.Colin Chong, Everton’s Chief Real Estate and Regeneration Officer, remarked: “From the outset, our ambition for Hill Dickinson Stadium extended far beyond delivering a new home for Everton Football Club. It was also about unlocking the potential of Liverpool’s northern waterfront and providing a catalyst for wider investment, regeneration and economic growth. “We are already seeing the positive impact of the stadium on the surrounding area, with new businesses establishing themselves and existing businesses benefiting from increased footfall and activity. “The updated Liverpool Waters masterplan provides an opportunity to build on that momentum. New public spaces, improved walking routes and better connectivity will complement our own investment in establishing Hill Dickinson Stadium and our Budweiser Plaza as a year-round destination, enhancing the appeal of the area, attracting more visitors and creating further opportunities for businesses, investment and employment across North Liverpool.” The growing programme of major sporting and entertainment events at Hill Dickinson Stadium is extending the economic benefits of Everton’s investment beyond football matchdays and across the wider Liverpool City Region. As well as being the home for Everton's Premier League fixtures, Hill Dickinson Stadium has already hosted an international football fixture between Scotland and Côte d’Ivoire, a Rugby League Ashes Test, Magic WKND and a Rugby Union Nations Championship fixture, the stadium will also host matches during UEFA EURO 2028, with a programme of major concerts at the Club’s waterfront home set to get under way in summer 2027. The ability to attract events of national and international significance is helping to further strengthen Liverpool’s reputation as a global sporting, cultural and entertainment destination, drawing additional visitors to the city, supporting its hotel, hospitality, retail and transport sectors, and creating further opportunities for investment and employment across the region. Since the original Liverpool Waters masterplan was approved in 2013, the northern waterfront has undergone significant change, with the delivery of new residential developments, transport infrastructure, leisure and hospitality destinations and public spaces, alongside Hill Dickinson Stadium and the Isle of Man Ferry Terminal. James Whittaker, Managing Director of Peel Waters, said: “The approval of the updated Liverpool Waters masterplan marks another major milestone in the transformation of Liverpool’s northern waterfront. Since the original masterplan was approved in 2013, we have delivered significant progress across the site, including new homes, public spaces, leisure destinations, major transport infrastructure and the new Everton Stadium, helping establish Liverpool Waters as one of the UK’s most ambitious regeneration projects. “This updated framework reflects the considerable investment already made by Peel Waters and our partners, while providing the flexibility needed to respond to evolving market demand and future opportunities. With over £81 million of infrastructure investment committed at Central Docks, Princes Dock nearing completion and a clear vision for future neighbourhoods, Liverpool Waters is entering an exciting new chapter that will continue to create homes, jobs, investment and opportunities for Liverpool and the wider city region.” The revised framework also strengthens commitments around sustainability, biodiversity, climate resilience and the preservation of Liverpool’s rich maritime heritage – principles that were central to the development of Everton’s waterfront home. Pete Swift, CEO and Co-Founder, Planit – the landscape architecture, urban design and masterplanning studio who also worked as part of the team to deliver Everton's new home, added: “We are overjoyed at the approval, not just for the Peel Waters and Liverpool Waters team but for the communities of Liverpool. “A network of green and blue spaces, with the central park at the heart, now forms the backbone for our neighbourhoods. We understand better the assets that sit below the ground and the history on and above it – views old and new structure the place. “Hill Dickinson stadium changes the game; literally – for Everton Football Club and North Liverpool. It was never in the original masterplan [from 2013] and so we must adapt to respond to it and the opportunities it brings. Our wider variety of homes now represents a more inclusive, family-focused, inter-generational Liverpool Waters. “Today’s consent embodies Peel Waters’ future-facing attitude and commitment to the quality of buildings and their supporting infrastructure – to remake a place that will play a major role in North Liverpool’s sustainable future.” The approved masterplan retains Liverpool Waters’ five-neighbourhood structure comprising Princes Dock, KINGS, Central Docks, Clarence Docks and Northern Docks. Liverpool Waters also sits within the proposed Liverpool City Region Mayoral Development Zone, an initiative designed to accelerate regeneration, support investment and unlock the delivery of new homes, jobs and infrastructure. The approval of Peel Waters' updated masterplan represents the next stage in the evolution of Liverpool’s northern waterfront, building on the investment made by Everton in delivering Hill Dickinson Stadium and the Club’s longstanding ambition for its new home to be a driver of economic growth, regeneration and lasting opportunities for North Liverpool and the wider city region.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, an ultimately routine Arsenal win but, even by the standards of VAR, an utterly bizarre refereeing controversy. Mikel Arteta’s instant simmering fury at being denied a first-half penalty may also have turned into something rather more explosive had Martin Odegaard not later sent the champions six points clear with a ninth win in 10 Premier League games.

Sources indicate that the major talking point arose with inadvertent theatre from referee Farai Hallam when Kai Havertz, who was clearly in an offside position, was equally clearly pulled down by Hull City defender Nobel Mendy inside the penalty area. Which came first? The intervention of VAR suggested the latter. But Hallam duly went to check the pitch-side monitor before then announcing the former.

Sources indicate that “After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No 32 on Red No 29,” the referee declared. Cue cheers from the home Arsenal crowd. “However…,” he went on. “Red No 29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City.”.

#ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

It all sounded so decisive that most inside the Emirates instinctively thought the outcome reasonable. But then came a closer look at the rules. And Law 11.2 certainly did seem to support Arteta’s protestations: “In situations where a player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”.

Industry observers note that arteta clearly saw no value after the match in aiming much criticism at Hallam following a fourth 1-0 win in 10 league games, but did still emphasise his surprise at the decision. “What do you think?” he asked one reporter. “I thought offside, but the law states that doesn’t matter,” replied the journalist. “So not offside then,” said Arteta, who stressed that he needs to understand “what is overruling what in the decision-making” after a Premier League statement simply said that Havertz was deemed offside “in the build-up”.

At the very best, it all leaves further confusion and again opens refereeing body Pro Ref to the charge of inconsistency. Fabian Schär, for example, was awarded a penalty for Newcastle against Bournemouth in 2024, despite being in an offside position when his shirt was grabbed by Adam Smith.

Conversely, Dango Ouattara had a penalty overturned for Brentford against Leeds last season after going down under pressure from Gabriel Gudmundsson before being deemed offside. The crucial point seems to be whether the player has actually challenged for the ball at the time of the infringement and, in this case, the answer was surely “no”.

Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace manufacturer Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.
  • The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.
  • It has been revealed that "I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace manufacturer Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

It has been revealed that "I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business.".

It has been revealed that he also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.

An Airbus spokesperson told DW the manufacturer is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments.".

Airbus and the US company Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.

The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

Recent findings suggest that she says because the issue is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she remarked.

At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

In a recent development, "The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors.".

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It says it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.

A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, says the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.

Another potential concern is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak indicates it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.

"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen.".

In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

Sources indicate that "The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things.".

He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

"Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously.".

It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' plan to develop a newly introduced single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce.".

She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

Sources indicate that "I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak noted. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union.".

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.

"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he remarked. "That in itself is an escalatory development.".

  • Everton has confirmed a new multi-year partnership with WTW, a leading global advisory, broking and solutions company, as the Club continues to expand its commercial portfolio into new categories.
  • The agreement sees WTW become Everton’s ‘Official Insurance Partner’, bringing specialist expertise in insurance, risk management and analytics to support the Club’s operations and long-term ambitions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that everton has confirmed a upcoming multi-year partnership with WTW, a leading global advisory, broking and solutions firm, as the Club continues to expand its commercial portfolio into new categories. The agreement sees WTW become Everton’s ‘Official Insurance Partner’, bringing specialist expertise in insurance, risk management and analytics to support the Club’s operations and long-term ambitions. Operating across more than 140 countries and markets, WTW becomes the latest internationally-recognised business to join Everton’s growing partnership portfolio, following recent agreements with NOCO, Nestlé and JYSK. Through the agreement, WTW will benefit from brand visibility at Hill Dickinson Stadium and across Everton’s digital and social media channels as well as commercial activation opportunities through access to the Club’s waterfront home for client hospitality, business events and engagement activities. The agreement allows for wider collaboration, including community initiatives, that will also be explored. As Everton’s exclusive partner in the insurance brokerage category, WTW will also provide tailored risk and insurance advice and solutions, drawing on its global insurance-market relationships and extensive experience across the sports and entertainment industry. Mark Rollings, Chief Partnerships Officer at Everton, noted: “We are delighted to welcome WTW as our Official Insurance Partner. “WTW is a highly respected global business with an outstanding reputation for expertise and innovation. Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.
  • Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.
  • "Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.

Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.

"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.

Sources indicate that "Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp said, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves.".

Recent findings suggest that the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.

It paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.

In a recent development, the 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.

"I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp remarked after the Netherlands match.

"We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired.".

That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.

Sources indicate that but Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.

"They can both play, my goodness," said Klopp.

Scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.

In a recent development, "A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still mentioned it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.

"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong.".

According to recent reports, proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he said, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer.".

While that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.

According to recent reports, "We've been through a tough time," he said. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it.".

Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.

In a recent development, "We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he remarked.

It has been revealed that in Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.

Latest Update: Can smart cities attract the talent they need to thrive?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, more than half of the world’s population now lives in cities, and that figure is projected to increase to nearly 70% by 2050.
  • As the global competition for talent and investment intensifies, many governments see these new cities and urban areas as strategic resources for boosting their innovative and economic competitiveness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, robots compete in a football event during RoboCup 2026, a robotics and AI competition held at the Songdo Convensia convention centre in Incheon, South Korea. Credit: Ahn Young-joon/Associated Press/ALAMY.

In a recent development, more than half of the world’s population now lives in cities, and that figure is projected to increase to nearly 70% by 2050. With the numbers of urban dwellers set to expand rapidly in some regions, a new generation of towns and cities is on the rise: communities that are designed to be cleaner and more efficient, driven by a host of technologies such as artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things — a network of sensors and devices that collect and transmit data about their surroundings.

As the global competition for talent and investment intensifies, many governments see these new cities and urban areas as strategic resources for boosting their innovative and economic competitiveness. Research facilities, both public and private, are central to this strategy.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

According to recent reports, in Songdo, South Korea — an early experiment in building a smart city from the ground up — biopharmaceutical giants such as Samsung Biologics have built major manufacturing facilities, and academic institutions such as Yonsei University have set up training and research centres to nurture scientists. In Hengqin, a rapidly developing district in the Pearl River Delta of southern China, research institutions also play a key role in a government strategy aimed at attracting talent, diversifying the economy and building a reputation for high-tech innovation.

Recent findings suggest that for some researchers, purpose-built tech-centric cities provide them with the ideal environment to conduct experiments. Air-quality and traffic-flow research benefits greatly from consistent, real-time data gathered from many different locations, for instance. “Smart cities can offer something very valuable: a real-world laboratory,” notes Dakota McCarty, a researcher of urban planning at George Mason University’s Songdo campus.

It has been revealed that but building a liveable city from scratch takes more than implementing advanced technologies and creating favourable conditions for institutions. Many large-scale urban projects across the world are facing a collective challenge: how to convince talented people to live there?

It has been revealed that the term ‘smart cities’ generally refers to places that are made to run more efficiently and sustainably through the extensive use of digital technologies. Songdo, located about 40 kilometres southwest of South Korea’s capital, Seoul, is often described as “the world’s first smart city”1. The idea for Songdo dates back to the 1980s, but construction did not begin until several years after the 1998 Asian financial crisis, when the Incheon metropolitan government proposed developing Songdo as part of a free economic zone aimed at attracting foreign investment2. Today, Songdo spans about 5,260 hectares of coastal land, roughly the size of Manhattan.

Recent findings suggest that in 2011, a series of futuristic technologies was built into Songdo’s infrastructure as part of South Korea’s campaign to establish ‘ubiquitous cities’, its name for smart cities at the time. One example is its underground waste-collection system — a network of subterranean pipes that suck rubbish directly from individual households, rather than transporting it by road. The system uses bins fitted with sensors and built into the stairwells of residential buildings. Once the sensors detect that the bins are full, the system will automatically empty them and send the rubbish through the pipes to a waste centre. Recyclable rubbish is cleaned and reused, and food waste is processed into compost.

In addition to the use of sensors in waste disposal, Songdo has deployed thousands of sensors to help manage other city functions such as traffic and security. These sensor networks link to a control centre run by the Incheon Free Economic Zone Authority (IFEZA), which manages Songdo and two other free economic zones in Incheon.

Recent findings suggest that extensive sensor networks and integrated data systems are a major asset for Songdo’s researchers and students, indicates McCarty, who moved from the United States to South Korea nearly a decade ago and has spent the past three years in Songdo. “In a place like Songdo, which was planned from the start with smart infrastructure, and has universities, industry and public agencies relatively close together, there is much more potential to test ideas in real urban conditions,” he says.

Industry observers note that data can be accessed through a website run by IFEZA, with additional data sets available on request. McCarty and his students are combining traffic data obtained from IFEZA with observations collected on the ground to build a model of Songdo’s walkability. The team hopes to show that adjusting traffic-light timings could make the city more accommodating for pedestrians without increasing congestion3.

Sources indicate that there is a downside to building a city’s renown around cutting-edge technology, however: other cities can catch up. As the novelty of Songdo’s original smart-city infrastructure started to fade, it increasingly sought to build its identity around industry clusters that are harder for competitors to replicate.

According to recent reports, biopharmaceuticals, for example, is a strategic industry for South Korea, with the government committing US$1.5 billion to support the sector over this decade. Celltrion, one of South Korea’s largest biotechnology companies, was among the first firms of its kind to commit to Songdo in 2003. Samsung Biologics, a major biopharmaceutical manufacturer, established its headquarters there in 2011.

It has been revealed that moves like this helped to create a new development path for the city, claims Sohyun Park, a researcher of economic geography at George Mason University in Songdo. “As these firms expanded, local and national governments increasingly concentrated resources on developing Songdo as a biotechnology cluster,” says Park. As of 2021, Songdo was home to around 60 biotechnology companies, and the government’s initiative is to expand that number to 700 by 2030.

Dakota McCarty and his team at George Mason University’s Songdo campus are using traffic data to come up with ways to make the city more pedestrian-friendly.Credit: Dakota McCarty / George Mason University Korea.

Recent findings suggest that such expansion depends on the support of Songdo’s university sector to train a fresh generation of biomedical talent. Yonsei University, which has its main campus in Seoul and an international campus in Songdo, opened the Korean National Institute for Bioprocessing Research and Training (K-NIBRT) in Songdo last year. The project has received around 60.9 billion South Korean won (US$41 million) from national and regional authorities and aims to train 2,000 biopharmaceutical specialists each year to address labour shortages locally and across the country.

Sources indicate that K-NIBRT benefits from Songdo’s complete biopharmaceuticals value chain, claims Gyoonhee Han, the institution’s director-general, because its research institutes, drug manufacturers and raw material and equipment suppliers are all conveniently packed into a radius of a 10-minute drive. This tight-knit ecosystem means that companies, researchers and academics can collaborate efficiently where industry is located, and trainees are able to enter the workforce as soon as they graduate, says Han.

Beyond biopharmaceuticals, Songdo intends on expanding its university base more broadly, particularly within its Incheon Global Campus (IGC), a higher-education zone established in the early 2010s and backed by US$1 billion in investment from the Korean and Incheon Metropolitan City governments. Campuses of three US universities — George Mason University, the University of Utah and the State University of New York (which has two Songdo campuses) — plus Belgium’s Ghent University have opened in the IGC, and six more universities are expected to join in the coming years.

Songdo’s evolution reflects a broader challenge for smart-city projects: advanced technologies and digital infrastructure can attract investment and attention, but long-term R&D activity depends on assets that are harder to build: universities, skilled workforces and specialized industry clusters.

According to recent reports, in Hengqin, an island in southern China’s Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA), regional and central governments are trying to combine both approaches. In addition to the autonomous-vehicle technologies that Hengqin and the wider GBA area are known for — including driverless buses, taxis and delivery services — universities and research institutes are being positioned at the centre of Hengqin’s development strategy.

Sources indicate that hengqin entered a upcoming phase of cross-border cooperation in 2009, when China’s central government passed legislation enabling Macau, a special administrative region with its own governance system, to exercise jurisdiction over part of the neighbouring island. The goal was to allow the University of Macau to move its campus away from a densely populated casino hub, and more broadly to have Hengqin serve as a bridge between Macau and the neighbouring Guangdong province.

These efforts were accelerated in 2021, when China established the Guangdong–Macao In-Depth Cooperation Zone — an economic and administrative area covering more than 100 km2 of Hengqin, run jointly by the Macau and Guangdong governments. One of the biggest projects within this fresh zone is an international university town, expected to be completed by 2030 at a cost of nearly 20 billion Macau pataca (US$2.47 billion). At least three universities plan to open campuses there — the University of Macau (which will build an additional campus alongside an existing one), Macao Polytech University and Macao University of Tourism — to accommodate roughly 20,000 students.

Students develop flexible electronics in the Soft Sensors-Actuators-Robots Laboratory at the University of Macau’s main campus in Hengqin.Credit: The University of Macau.

Recent findings suggest that “Academic and research capabilities are essential, because they provide the talent, knowledge and innovation infrastructure that Hengqin needs to become a science and technology hub,” claims Yonghua Song, president of the Macao Association for Higher Education Development and rector of the University of Macau. Song adds that new facilities such as the University of Macau’s Faculty of Information Science and Computing, opened in August, are expected to train talent in highly competitive areas such as artificial intelligence, microelectronics and financial technology.

According to recent reports, like Songdo, researchers in Hengqin benefit from its extensive smart-city infrastructure, including the large networks of sensors in operation across the island. According to Ma Shaodan, a wireless-communications researcher at the University of Macau’s State Key Laboratory of Internet of Things for Smart City in Hengqin, having smart-city infrastructure right outside the laboratory removes many of the constraints of conventional research environments. “It provides an invaluable physical context that accelerates our research, strengthens our regional impact, and serves as a tangible blueprint to inspire the next generation of engineers,” she indicates.

Early signs suggest that Hengqin’s strategy to become a place of high-tech innovation is gaining momentum: the University of Macau has expanded its presence, research infrastructure has proliferated and authorities continue to invest heavily in the cooperation zone.

The ballot application window for Forever Blue+ Members for the Sunderland fixture will open on Monday 30 November at 10am. Ballot applications can be submitted online, over the phone on 0151 556 1878, or in person at the Hill Dickinson South Stand box office. Supporters will have until 4pm on Tuesday 1 December to submit their application. Box office opening times can be found here. Supporters wishing to enter the ballot during this priority period can gain access by signing up for a Forever Blue+ membership here. Forever Blue Members can also upgrade to a Forever Blue+ membership by calling the Everton Fan Centre on 0151 556 1878 and quoting their membership/supporter number. Eligible supporters will be able to apply individually or in a group of up to six family and friends (please note, all supporters within a group must meet the eligibility criteria for the ballot). Each membership/supporter number can only be entered into a ballot once. Therefore, if a membership/supporter number is included as part of a group application, it cannot then be used for a separate individual application or an application as part of another group. Tickets are limited to one per Member. Supporters should note that, in order to accrue an individual booking history, unique supporter numbers must be given for each attending supporter. Successful applicants will receive confirmation of their ticket by Thursday 3 December. Should any tickets remain, a second sales window will open at 10am on Friday 4 December for Forever Blue Members. Forever Blue+ Members who did not enter the ballot, or whose ballot entry was unsuccessful, will also be eligible to purchase tickets during this sales window. Official ticket and hotel packages for all Everton Premier League home fixtures are available via Sportsbreaks.com. Packages include an official match ticket in Block 204 or 206, plus a minimum one-night stay in a handpicked Liverpool hotel, including breakfast. Official Premium experiences for all Everton Premier League home fixtures are available via seatunique.com It is an offence under Section 166 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 for any unauthorised person to resell tickets. Further information regarding the Club's stance against Ticket Touting can be seen here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Francisco Conceição has been offered to Newcastle United, and Juventus could look to use the winger to help keep Nick Woltemade beyond this season.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, via TuttoMercatoWeb, Conceição’s agent Jorge Mendes has put his client’s name forward to the Magpies ahead of next summer.

Industry observers note that no talks have taken place yet, but the Portuguese winger isn’t short of admirers in England. Liverpool and Manchester United both made enquiries about him in the summer, without following them up.

Woltemade is the key as the German striker joined the Bianconeri late in the summer window on a straight loan from Newcastle, which expires on 30 June 2027 with no option to buy. If Juventus want to keep him, they will have to negotiate a newly introduced deal with the Premier League club, and Newcastle’s interest in Conceição could give them leverage on the price.

Selling him would also make financial sense. By next summer, the 24-year-old will be on Juventus’ books for less than €20 million, so any fee above that would be a significant capital gain.

The player himself, however, is happy in Turin and has no aims to leave. Luciano Spalletti also sees him as an crucial part of his attack.

Conceição has been out for around 40 days with a left shoulder problem, but is fit again and is expected to start on the right against Omonia in the Europa League tonight. Kick-off at the Allianz Stadium is at 21:00 CET [20:00 GMT]. You can follow all the action, as it happens, on our Live Blog.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this Christmas, Everton in the Community is calling on supporters to help tackle loneliness and bring the true Christmas Spirit of the Blues to those who need it most. Loneliness can affect anyone, at any time of the year. It could be an older person facing another Christmas without their loved ones, a young person struggling to find where they belong, a parent finding it difficult to cope or someone surrounded by people but still feeling alone. That's why the official charitable arm of Everton Football Club is launching Christmas Spirit of the Blues, a campaign dedicated to raising awareness of loneliness in all its forms and ensuring everyone knows there is somewhere they can turn. Dedicated to breaking down barriers and supporting its local community since 1988, Everton in the Community delivers more than 50 inclusive, free programmes, each designed to tackle different societal challenges. From supporting young people back into education and giving fresh fathers access to vital support networks, to helping military veterans navigate life after the forces, each programme shares the same ambition - to improve confidence, provide a sense of belonging and remind people just how crucial they are. To launch the campaign, Everton in the Community brought together participants, staff, supporters and players past and present at Hill Dickinson Stadium for a special performance of the iconic Liverpool Express hit, Spirit of the Blues. Liverpool-based brass band Allerton Brass performed a slowed-down version of the track, creating a poignant moment of togetherness and highlighting the power of music to bring people together. Throughout the build-up to Christmas, the campaign will shine a light on the experiences of people who have faced loneliness and explore how finding support, friendship and a sense of belonging has made a difference to their lives. Among those sharing their stories is Gina, who has found cherished friendships through Everton in the Community's Stand Together programme following the loss of her husband, and a young man whose experience of loneliness brought him to the brink of suicide. The campaign will also hear from father-of-two Sean, who reached out to Everton in the Community in the middle of the night after his wife tragically died just 12 hours after giving birth to their second son. “My newborn baby and his two-year-old brother were asleep, and I found myself feeling completely alone, drowning in grief and crying uncontrollably. “It was a hail Mary. I just needed to reach out to someone and, as an Evertonian, I knew about Everton in the Community – but I didn't expect the level of help I did get. It was a lifesaver.”  At a time when his world had been turned upside down, Sean says reaching out gave him someone to turn to when he felt he had nowhere else to go, and marked the first step towards navigating life without his wife. Dan Halliday, Head of Fundraising at Everton in the Community, noted: “For thousands of people across the Liverpool City Region and beyond, loneliness, social isolation and grief can feel even heavier at Christmas. “The pressure to feel happy or the absence of familiar handwriting on a Christmas card can be painful reminders of what's missing. “This Christmas, a donation to Everton in the Community could help someone feel seen, supported and part of something bigger. Together, we can make sure nobody has to face loneliness alone.”  To donate to Everton in the Community and join our mission to end loneliness together, visit (insert link). For more information about accessing support, visit https://www.evertoninthecommunity.org/projects/minds/accessing-mental-health-support/.

Throughout the build-up to Christmas, the campaign will shine a light on the experiences of people who have faced loneliness and explore how finding support, friendship and a sense of belonging has made a difference to their lives.

Among those sharing their stories is Gina, who has found cherished friendships through Everton in the Community's Stand Together programme following the loss of her husband, and a young man whose experience of loneliness brought him to the brink of suicide.

The campaign will also hear from father-of-two Sean, who reached out to Everton in the Community in the middle of the night after his wife tragically died just 12 hours after giving birth to their second son.

“My newborn baby and his two-year-old brother were asleep, and I found myself feeling completely alone, drowning in grief and crying uncontrollably.

It has been revealed that “It was a hail Mary. I just needed to reach out to someone and, as an Evertonian, I knew about Everton in the Community – but I didn't expect the level of help I did get. It was a lifesaver.”.

At a time when his world had been turned upside down, Sean indicates reaching out gave him someone to turn to when he felt he had nowhere else to go, and marked the first step towards navigating life without his wife.

Dan Halliday, Head of Fundraising at Everton in the Community, said: “For thousands of people across the Liverpool City Region and beyond, loneliness, social isolation and grief can feel even heavier at Christmas.

“The pressure to feel happy or the absence of familiar handwriting on a Christmas card can be painful reminders of what's missing.

“This Christmas, a donation to Everton in the Community could help someone feel seen, supported and part of something bigger. Together, we can make sure nobody has to face loneliness alone.”.

To donate to Everton in the Community and join our mission to end loneliness together, visit (insert link).

For more information about accessing support, visit https://www.evertoninthecommunity.org/projects/minds/accessing-mental-health-support/.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Published: 13:49 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 14:19 EST, 26 November 2026.
  • The SFA have been forced back to the drawing board for a second time in their efforts to introduce newly introduced proposals around youth development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 13:49 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 14:19 EST, 26 November 2026.

The SFA have been forced back to the drawing board for a second time in their efforts to introduce newly introduced proposals around youth development.

Led by chief football officer Craig Mulholland, the prepares had been geared towards ensuring more Under-21 players in Scotland gain more minutes at first-team level.

The original aims were for two Scotland-eligible Under-21 players to start in domestic cup competitions, and for players to feature for a minimum of six per cent of all available minutes across a season in league campaigns.

When it became clear that several clubs in Scotland weren’t on board, a new watered-down version was put back on the table.

But the latest proposals have also now been met with resistance — forcing the SFA to kick the can further down the road into the new year.

There will now be no vote on the back of the upcoming AGM, with further discussions required prior to something more concrete coming to fruition for the start of next season.

SFA chief football officer Craig Mulholland has been sent back to the drawing board by clubs.

A statement from the governing body said: ‘The Scottish FA has been encouraged by the productive dialogue with clubs regarding proposals to harness opportunities for young homegrown talent.

‘The most recent discussions have spawned a range of additional potential innovations that all parties agree will require further consultation in order to present a consolidated package of recommendations to an SPFL member vote.

‘The passion we all have for Scottish football has been demonstrated by the public debate sparked since the all-club meeting in St Andrews, when the reality of our domestic game’s standing in respect of playing time for under-21 players compared to the rest of Europe was made clear.

‘We will continue to engage in dialogue with the aim of delivering a proposal that will achieve the stated objective of improving opportunities for young homegrown players to fulfil their potential at the top end of the Scottish professional game.

‘It is an objective everyone benefits from: players, clubs, supporters and Scotland national teams.

‘We have therefore agreed that the consultation process will continue into the Newly introduced Year with the intention of a comprehensive proposal going to SPFL members within the first quarter of 2027, in time for the start of William Hill SPFL season 2027-28.

‘The Scottish FA General Meeting to vote on the complementary Scottish Gas Men’s Scottish Cup proposals will now follow a similar timetable.

‘Given the implications for our game, and our young talent, it is imperative that we take the necessary time to get those proposals right.’.

Very warm reception for Elliot Anderson from the Forest fans as he runs to the tunnel leading to the dressing rooms.

Anderson was at Forest for two seasons before that £116m move to Manchester City.

Man City will be hoping to close the gap on Arsenal to three points at the top of the table after the north London side’s 1-0 win over Hull City this afternoon.

Forest’s results at the City Ground have to improve swiftly or this team will be in serious trouble.

Recent findings suggest that “If you never say anything in your relationship with your wife or children, then they will never know. Then I can’t blame somebody because if they don’t know, how can you expect things to change?

“We are now in a society where criticism or the way I talk is negative, but the intention was positive and to change to get better results so that we can all have a better life.”.

Gianluigi Donnarumma, who has made three errors leading to goals this season, “recognises that he has made some mistakes,” Enzo Maresca said this week, “but at the same time recognises that he has made some great saves”.

Asked about City players adapting to his philosophy, Maresca stated: “I can see my playing style just by working every day with them, but we can still improve many things.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Representatives of Serbia's student-led movement were sworn in as lawmakers on Tuesday, just over four weeks after they ended Serbia's strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic's 14 years of rule.

The Students' List candidates officially took their seats in the inaugural parliamentary session as the first step for the youth-backed party toward forming Serbia's latest government.

In a recent development, the movement holds 140 seats in the 250-member parliament while Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) holds 103. The remaining seats belong to ethnic minority parties.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Hundreds gathered outside the parliament building in the capital Belgrade, to show their support for the student-backed lawmakers, most of whom are teachers, professors and other professionals with little or no political experience.

Meanwhile, SNS candidates were met with a negative reaction from the crowd. A woman in the crowd poured yogurt over an SNS member's head as she climbed the steps to the parliament entrance.

According to Serbian media, the newly elected lawmakers have been preparing for their first session for days. They will face veteran opposition politicians, including Aleksandar Vucic, who became the opposition leader after his defeat.

The Students' List will have 90 days to name a prime minister, present their programme and form a government, once the parliament is formed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, the movement unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

They pledged to improve healthcare, boost education and double the defense budget, along with many other reforms.

Industry observers note that the election of a new parliamentary speaker will also lead to the appointment of a new acting president. The speaker has held the role since Vucic resigned in September to run for prime minister.

A snap presidential election must be called by November 27 and held by December 27.

Both parties are expected to put forward presidential candidates, but Vucic cannot seek another term because the constitution limits presidents to two terms in office.
